01.note: Rav Mari, the son of Shmuel's daughter, describes what he saw during the famine at the moment Rav Yehuda's fast brought rain. Standing on the bank of the Pappa River, he saw angels disguised as sailors filling ships with sand, and the sand turned into fine flour. Everyone came to buy it, but he told them not to, because it was the product of miracles; boats full of wheat would arrive from Parzina the next day, and they could buy that instead.
01.why: The Gemara has just told how Rav Yehuda ended a famine by removing one shoe in distress; Rav Mari's account adds what he witnessed at that very moment.

people.name: Rav Mari
people.about: The son of Shmuel's daughter; he tells what he saw on the river bank and warns people not to buy the miraculous flour.

terms.meaning: Something that came into being through a miracle rather than in the ordinary way. Rav Mari tells people not to buy and use such flour, and to wait for ordinary wheat.

02.note: Rava came to the town of Hagrunya and decreed a fast, but no rain came. He told everyone to keep fasting through the night, and the next morning asked whether anyone had had a dream. Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya said these words had been recited to him in his dream: Good greetings to a good master from a good Lord, Who in His goodness does good for His people. Rava concluded that it was a favorable time to pray; he prayed, and rain came.
02.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages who fasted and prayed for rain, after Rabba's complaint that his generation cries out and is not answered; here a dream reveals the right moment and the prayer succeeds.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage visiting Hagrunya who decrees a fast for rain.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya
people.about: A local man who reports the dream with its message of good greetings.

terms.meaning: When rain failed, a leader could order the community to fast and pray together, as a public act of repentance and pleading for rain.

03.note: A man sentenced by Rava's court to flogging for relations with a gentile woman was flogged and died. King Shapur of Persia heard and wanted to punish Rava, but his mother, Ifra Hormiz, told him not to quarrel with the Jews, since their God gives them whatever they ask. When the king said rain after prayer was only the season, she sent word to Rava to pray for rain in the summer month of Tammuz. He prayed, but no rain came. Then he cried that his ancestors had told of God's wonders but he had not seen them, and rain fell until the gutters of Mehoza poured into the Tigris. His father appeared in a dream, rebuked him for troubling Heaven so much, and told him to change where he slept. He did, and the next day found his bed slashed by knives.
03.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages whose prayers for rain were or were not answered; this one puts such a prayer to a test set by a foreign king.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Head of the court that flogged the man; he prays for rain at the queen mother's request.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: The Persian king, who wants to punish Rava and doubts that Jewish prayer brings rain.

people.name: Ifra Hormiz
people.about: King Shapur's mother, who warns him not to quarrel with the Jews and asks Rava to pray.

terms.meaning: A summer month in the Jewish calendar, a dry season when rain does not normally fall in the region.
The Talmud's usual phrase for praying to God for help in a time of need.

04.note: Rav Pappa decreed a fast, but no rain came. Feeling faint, he swallowed a bowl of porridge and prayed, and still no rain came. Rav Nahman bar Ushpazti mocked him: if the Master swallows another bowl of porridge, rain will come. Rav Pappa was embarrassed and upset, and then the rain came.
04.why: The Gemara is collecting stories of fasts for rain; here it is the leader's shame and broken heart, not the fast itself, that brings the rain.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who decreed a fast for rain and ate during it when he grew weak.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Ushpazti
people.about: The man who mocks Rav Pappa for eating porridge during the fast.

05.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was traveling on a road when it began to rain. He said to God: the whole world is comfortable, and Hanina is suffering. The rain stopped. When he reached home he said: the whole world is suffering, and Hanina is comfortable? The rain began again.
05.why: Rav Yosef reacts by asking what the High Priest's yearly prayer, that God ignore the prayers of travelers, can do against Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa, whose traveler's prayer was answered at once.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose prayers stop and restart the rain.

terms.meaning: A common way of addressing God directly in prayer.

06.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's family was so poor that his wife heated an empty oven every Friday so the smoke would hide their poverty. An evil neighbor, knowing they had nothing, knocked on the door to see what was baking, and the embarrassed wife went into an inner room. A miracle happened: the neighbor saw the oven full of bread and the kneading basin full of dough, and called out to her to bring a shovel because her bread was burning. The wife answered that she had gone inside for that very purpose. A teacher of the early tradition adds that she had indeed gone to fetch a shovel, because she was used to miracles.
06.why: The Gemara has just quoted a Divine Voice saying the whole world is sustained by Hanina's merit while he lives on a small measure of carobs a week; this story shows that poverty, and the miracles that met it.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage, desperately poor; the story concerns his household.

terms.meaning: A Sage of the early period whose teachings were handed down as authoritative tradition; 'a tanna taught' introduces such a teaching.
Friday, when bread is baked for the Sabbath.

06.flag: The story begins mid-sentence ('due to embarrassment'); its opening, the wife heating the empty oven, sits in the preceding segment.

07.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's wife asked how long they would go on suffering poverty, and urged him to pray that something be given to him. He prayed, and something like the palm of a hand came out and gave him one leg of a golden table. That night she dreamed that in the World-to-Come the righteous would eat at golden tables with three legs, while she would eat at one with two. He asked whether she was content to eat at a defective table; she told him to pray for the leg to be taken back. He prayed, and it was taken. A teaching adds that the last miracle was greater than the first, since by tradition Heaven gives but does not take back.
07.why: The Gemara is telling a run of stories about Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's poverty and the wonders around him; this one shows him choosing poverty now over a lessened reward later.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor and righteous Sage whose prayers are answered.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where the righteous receive their reward.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written collection of Jewish law.

08.note: One Friday evening Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa saw that his daughter was sad. She told him she had mixed up a jar of vinegar with a jar of oil and lit the Sabbath lamp with vinegar. He told her not to worry: the One who told oil to burn can tell vinegar to burn. A teaching adds that the lamp burned all through the next day, until they took light from it for havdala.
08.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of the wonders that surrounded the poor, righteous Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage who reassures his daughter that God can make vinegar burn.

terms.meaning: The short ceremony at the end of the Sabbath, recited over a cup of wine and a flame, that marks the passage from holy time to the ordinary week.

09.note: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa owned some goats, and people told him they were causing damage. He said: if they are doing damage, let bears eat them; if not, let each one bring home a bear on its horns this evening. That evening each goat came home with a bear on its horns.
09.why: The Gemara next asks how the poor Rabbi Hanina came to own goats, which the Sages forbade raising in the Land of Israel, and answers with another story about where they came from.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose goats are accused of grazing on others' property.

10.note: A neighbor of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa was building a house, but her ceiling beams were too short to reach the walls. She came to him and told him so. He asked her name; she said Ikku, and he said: if so, may your beams reach. A teaching says the beams then stretched until they stuck out a cubit on each side; some say pieces were added on. The Sage Palaimo is quoted as saying he saw the house himself, with its beams jutting out a cubit on each side, and was told it was the house Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa had roofed by his prayer.
10.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of the wonders that surrounded Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa; Palaimo's testimony that he saw the house himself caps the list.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A righteous Sage whose blessing lengthens his neighbor's beams.

people.name: Ikku
people.about: His neighbor, whose ceiling beams were too short.

people.name: Palaimo
people.about: A Sage who says he saw the house and its jutting beams.

terms.meaning: The woman's name; it sounds like the Aramaic for 'if so', and Rabbi Hanina plays on it in his blessing.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a meter.

11.note: A man had left chickens at the door of Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa's house, and his wife found them. Rabbi Hanina told her not to eat their eggs. The eggs hatched into many chickens, and since they were a nuisance, the family sold them and bought goats with the money. Later the same man passed by and told a companion that this was where he had left his chickens. Rabbi Hanina heard, asked whether he had an identifying sign, and when the man gave it, he took the goats. The Gemara concludes that these were the very goats that brought home bears on their horns.
11.why: The Gemara asked how the poor Rabbi Hanina could own goats, when the Sages forbade raising small animals in the Land of Israel; Rav Pinehas answers with this story, showing the goats were never really his.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa
people.about: A poor, righteous Sage who keeps a stranger's lost chickens safe for him.

terms.meaning: An identifying mark or detail by which an owner proves that a lost item is his, so it can be returned to him.

12.note: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat was very poor. After a bloodletting he had nothing to eat but a clove of garlic; he grew faint and fell asleep. The Sages who came to visit saw him weeping and laughing, with a ray of light shining from his forehead. When he woke he told them he had dreamed that God sat with him. He asked how long he would suffer in this world, and God offered to start the world over so he might be born at a lucky hour. Learning that most of his life was already behind him, he refused. As a reward God promised him thirteen rivers of balsam oil in the World-to-Come. He asked whether that was all, and God asked what then He would give his colleagues. He replied that he was not asking from a person who lacks. God flicked his forehead and said: Elazar, my son, My arrows upon you.
12.why: The Gemara has turned from Rabbi Hanina ben Dosa to more stories of desperately poor righteous people, and this is one of them.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A desperately poor Sage who tells of his dream conversation with God.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who in Rabbi Elazar's dream offers to remake the world and then promises him a reward.

terms.meaning: Drawing blood as a medical treatment; afterward a person was expected to eat to regain strength.
A precious perfumed oil, prized in the ancient world.

13.note: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina decreed a fast, but no rain came. People asked why, when Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had decreed a fast and rain had come. He answered that he was not Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. They suggested that everyone focus their minds together, so the community's hearts might break and rain would come. They prayed, and still no rain came. He asked whether they wanted rain to come for their sake, and they said yes. He called out: Skies, skies, cover your face. Nothing happened. He said: how impudent is the face of the sky! The sky clouded over, and rain came.
13.why: After stories of poor righteous men, the Gemara returns to its series of fasts for rain, showing the different ways a leader's prayer finally brought rain.

people.name: Rabbi Hama bar Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose fast for rain fails at first.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage mentioned as one whose fast for rain had been answered.

terms.meaning: A play on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's name ('ben Levi'), used by Rabbi Hama to say the two men are not of equal standing.

14.note: Levi decreed a fast, but no rain came. He said to God: You have gone up and sat on high, and You have no mercy on Your children. Rain came, but Levi became lame. Rav Elazar drew the lesson that a person should never hurl words toward Heaven, since a great man did so and became lame, and that man was Levi.
14.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of fasts for rain; this one shows that a bold prayer can bring rain yet cost the one who spoke it. The Gemara then asks whether Levi's lameness had a different cause.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage who rebukes God when his fast brings no rain, and becomes lame.

people.name: Rav Elazar
people.about: A Sage who draws the lesson from Levi's lameness.

15.note: Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani heard clouds saying to one another: let us go and bring water to Ammon and Moab. He said to God: when You gave the Torah to Your people Israel, You went around to all the nations of the world and they would not accept it, and now You are giving them rain? Throw it here. The clouds dropped their rain where they were.
15.why: The Gemara is gathering stories of Sages whose prayers brought rain; having named Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani, it goes on to quote his teaching on a verse.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Lulyani
people.about: A Sage who overhears the clouds and asks God to send their rain to Israel.

terms.meaning: Neighboring peoples across the Jordan River, east of the Land of Israel.

16.note: Rabbi Eliezer decreed thirteen fasts on the community, but no rain fell. At the end of the last fast, as the people began to leave, he said to them: have you prepared graves for yourselves? All the people burst into tears, and rain fell.
16.why: The Gemara has just finished a side discussion about cedars and returns to fasts for rain, quoting an early teaching with two incidents involving Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who leads the community through thirteen fasts for rain.

terms.meaning: The opening of a baraita, a teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna.

17.note: Rabbi Eliezer went down before the ark to lead the prayers on a fast day and recited twenty-four blessings, but he was not answered. Rabbi Akiva went down after him and said: Our Father, our King, we have no king but You; Our Father, our King, for Your sake have mercy on us. Rain fell. The Sages began to whisper, and a Divine Voice said: it is not because this one is greater than that one, but because this one is forgiving and that one is not.
17.why: It is the second of two early incidents about Rabbi Eliezer's fasts for rain; the Gemara then turns to how much rain must fall before a community may stop fasting.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage who leads the fast-day prayer and is not answered.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who prays after Rabbi Eliezer and is answered.

terms.meaning: To lead the congregation in prayer, standing before the cabinet that holds the Torah scrolls.
A voice from Heaven, which in the Talmud sometimes announces God's judgment.
Literally one who 'passes over his traits': a person who lets slights against him go rather than insisting on his due.

18.note: On another occasion Shmuel HaKatan decreed a fast, and rain fell only after sunset. The people thought this showed the community's merit. Shmuel told them it did not, and gave a parable: a slave asks his master for a reward, and the master tells his ministers to wait until the slave pines away and suffers, and only then give it to him.
18.why: It pairs with Shmuel HaKatan's earlier fast, when rain fell before sunrise and he also denied it showed merit; the Gemara then asks what, in his view, would count as a sign of the community's merit.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: A Sage who decreed a fast and refuses to read the timing of the rain as praise of the community.

terms.meaning: A short illustrative tale, often about a king or master and his servant, used to explain how God relates to people.

19.note: Only four of the twenty-four priestly watches came back from the exile in Babylonia: the families of Jedaiah, Harim, Pashhur and Immer. The prophets among the returnees divided them again into twenty-four watches. They mixed lots in a receptacle, and a representative of Jedaiah drew his own lot and five more, six in all; Harim did the same, and likewise Pashhur and Immer.
19.why: The Gemara is discussing how many priestly watches Moses first set up, and turns to a teaching on how the returning exiles rebuilt the full number of twenty-four.

people.name: Jedaiah
people.about: One of the four priestly families that returned from exile; its representative drew six lots.

people.name: Harim
people.about: One of the four returning priestly families.

people.name: Pashhur
people.about: One of the four returning priestly families.

people.name: Immer
people.about: One of the four returning priestly families.

terms.meaning: The priests were divided into groups, each serving in the Temple for one week in turn.

19.flag: The story starts mid-sentence ('and divided them'); its opening, the four watches that returned and the prophets among them, sits in the preceding segment. It reads more as a historical account than a story with characters.

20.note: When the exiles came back to Jerusalem, they found no wood in the Temple chamber for the altar, so certain families stood up and donated wood of their own. The prophets among them then laid down that these families would keep donating wood on their set days even if the chamber were full, citing the verse in Nehemiah about casting lots for the wood offering at appointed times year by year.
20.why: The mishna lists fixed days for the wood offering of priests and people; this early teaching explains why those days were set.

terms.meaning: Donations of firewood for the altar in the Temple, brought by particular families on fixed days of the year.
A storeroom in the Temple where wood for the altar was kept.

20.flag: This is an explanation of a custom's origin, with little narrative beyond the families' donation.
